title: He Survived Hiroshima. Then He Went Home to Nagasaki #shorts
description:
Case 010. In the summer of 1945 Tsutomu Yamaguchi, a 29-year-old engineer who designed ships for Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, was finishing a three-month work trip in Hiroshima. On the morning of 6 August the atomic bomb exploded about three kilometres from him. He was burned, his eardrums were ruptured and he was blinded for a time. He spent the night in an air-raid shelter and the next day made his way home to Nagasaki. On 9 August, bandaged, he reported for work and was describing the Hiroshima explosion to his boss, who did not believe that one bomb could destroy a city, when the second bomb exploded over Nagasaki. He was again about three kilometres away, and again he lived. He later worked as a translator, a teacher and once more as an engineer. In his last years he spoke publicly against nuclear weapons, including at the United Nations in 2006. In March 2009 the Japanese government recognised him as a survivor of both bombings, the only person it has officially recognised as one. He died of stomach cancer in Nagasaki on 4 January 2010, aged 93. Rook didn't believe it either.

The two bombings killed well over a hundred thousand people. This film follows one man's account and shows no one else; it is told with respect for all of them.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. The cards and maps in the film are drawings made for it, not real documents.

source_notes: Read for this run (fetched 14 Nov 2026): Wikipedia (Tsutomu Yamaguchi); the New York Times obituary of 6 Jan 2010 as reprinted by History News Network; ABC News (6 Jan 2010); Justin McCurry's report of 25 Mar 2009 as carried by the Canberra Times; The Week's obituary (which quotes the Daily Telegraph and The Times); Biography.com; an NPR interview transcript (2010). The Guardian, NYT, BBC and History.com pages themselves could not be opened by this run. Agreed by the sources that mention each point: born in Nagasaki on 16 March 1916, so 29 in August 1945 (NYT: 'a 29-year-old engineer for Mitsubishi Heavy Industries'); a ship/oil-tanker designer; in Hiroshima on a business trip of about three months; ruptured eardrums, burns, temporary blindness; a night in an air-raid shelter (Wikipedia, NYT, McCurry); home to Nagasaki the following day (Wikipedia, NYT, McCurry, Biography.com), by train (McCurry: he 'stumbled to the train station the next day'; NPR); reported for work on 9 August still bandaged (Wikipedia, Biography.com, NPR, The Week); was telling his boss about Hiroshima when the second bomb exploded (NYT, Wikipedia, McCurry, The Week, Biography.com); the boss did not believe him (McCurry: 'reportedly questioned his sanity'; The Week quotes Yamaguchi's own account of the boss's words; Wikipedia); thrown to the floor but not seriously hurt the second time; died in Nagasaki on 4 January 2010 aged 93 of stomach cancer; recognised by the Japanese government in March 2009 as a survivor of both bombings and the only person officially recognised as one (ABC, NYT, McCurry, The Week, Wikipedia); spoke against nuclear weapons late in life, including at the United Nations in 2006 (NYT, The Week, Wikipedia, ABC). Where the sources differ: (1) Distance in Hiroshima: 'about 3 km (1.9 mi)' (Wikipedia) or 'less than 2 miles' (NYT, Biography.com) or 'two miles' (NPR); these agree, and the script says 'under two miles' while the sketch says 'about 3 km'. (2) What he was doing at 8:15: walking toward the docks after going back for his personal seal (Wikipedia), getting off a streetcar (NYT), or in or beside a field ditch (Biography.com and NPR, both from Charles Pellegrino's book). The film shows him walking a road toward the shipyard and claims no more; the fields beside the road are set dressing. Nothing in the film rests on Pellegrino's book alone: those details reach us only through that one book. (3) Whether 6 August was the last day of the trip (Biography.com; Wikipedia says he was 'preparing to leave the city') or the day before he was due to leave (The Week, from the Telegraph). The script says only that he 'is ending a work trip'. (4) Burns: 'left side of the top half of his body' (Wikipedia), 'upper torso' (NYT), 'face and arms' (The Week, Biography.com), 'covering his body' (ABC). The film shows bandages on his head, left arm and shoulder and says only 'burned'. (5) The time in Nagasaki: Wikipedia's Yamaguchi article says he was talking to his supervisor at 11:00 a.m.; the time on record for the explosion is 11:02 (Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum; nagasakipeace.jp), which is what the clock insert shows. (6) How many people were under both bombs: 'about 165' (NYT, The Week, Wikipedia body), 'at least 160' (Wikipedia lead), or nine identified by a 2005 study (ABC). All agree he is the only one officially recognised as a double survivor, so the script says 'Officially, the only one' and gives no count. (7) The Week says he was knocked unconscious the second time; Wikipedia says unhurt but ill with fever and vomiting for over a week; the film shows him thrown down and getting up and the narration says 'He lives again'. (8) When he began to speak publicly: 'in his eighties' he wrote a memoir (Wikipedia), 'not until 2005' (The Week), 'until the 2000s' (Biography.com). The script says 'those years' and the description says 'his last years'. Paraphrased from his own words, not quoted: 'the same white light fills the room' follows his remark to The Independent (reported by the NYT) that the same white light filled the room. No dialogue is attributed to anyone and the boss's words are not given. Left out on purpose: everything about the dead and injured around him (the film stays with one man and shows no victims), his wife and children (sources disagree about whether his son had been born by August 1945), the illnesses of his later life and of his family, the two colleagues who were with him in Hiroshima and also survived (Wikipedia names them; the shelter scene shows him alone), the 2010 BBC QI controversy, and his meeting with James Cameron. Shown but not narrated, from the sources: the single aircraft and the two small parachutes he described seeing (his own account, in The Week and Wikipedia), 8:15 (the time on record for Hiroshima), the train, the bandages, his being thrown to the floor in the office, 11:02, the lectern (he spoke at the United Nations in 2006 after a screening of a documentary about double survivors), the dates 6 and 9 August 1945, March 2009, the ages 29 and 93. Dramatised, not reported: what the road, shipyard, shelter, station, train, office and hall looked like (all generic; the station board is blank, the locomotive and aircraft carry no numbers or markings, the hall is not a model of any real room and its audience is plain silhouettes); how he, his boss and the two draughtsmen looked and dressed; the bag he carries; the exact way he fell and stood up both times; the lantern; the luggage; the personnel file and the 'survivor record' card (both labelled in the film as drawn for it; the real certificate is not reproduced); the two sketch maps (labelled as sketches, not to scale); the far cloud (a plain low-poly column, deliberately not detailed); and everything Rook does. Rook is sceptical only in the first seven seconds. From the flash onward he makes no jokes, takes his hat off, and at the end he leaves a folded paper crane on the platform bench instead of pocketing a keepsake, because this is not a case to take a souvenir from; the crane is a general symbol of remembrance in Japan and is not tied to Yamaguchi by any source.
